title: Psalm 110: The King Who Is Also a Priest
summary: In a solemn oracle the LORD speaks to the psalmist's lord, the king, inviting him to sit at God's right hand until his enemies become his footstool, and sends his scepter out from Zion. God then swears an oath that this king is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. The psalm ends on the day of wrath, with the Lord at the king's right hand crushing kings, and the king drinking from a brook by the road and lifting up his head.
story:
Psalm 110 is the last of three psalms of David (108 to 110) that stand near the start of Book V, which opens with Psalm 107. Psalm 109 ended with God standing “at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from the condemners of his soul” (Psalm 109:31); Psalm 110 begins with a king invited to sit at God's right hand. The book's editors have set a king who is attacked and vindicated beside a king who is enthroned.

Book V was gathered for a people who had come back from exile without a king on David's throne. Psalm 89, at the end of Book III, had lamented that God cast the Davidic throne to the ground, and Books IV and V answer mostly by proclaiming that the LORD himself reigns. Psalm 110 keeps the royal promise alive inside that answer: a son of David enthroned beside God, ruling in the midst of enemies, and holding a priesthood God has sworn will never end. Jewish and Christian readers alike came to hear it as a promise about the Messiah, the anointed king to come.

No psalm, and no single Old Testament verse, is quoted or echoed more often in the New Testament than Psalm 110:1. It became the church's main text for saying that Jesus, raised from the dead, now reigns at the right hand of God, and through Hebrews verse 4 became its main text for Christ's priesthood. The church's creeds still confess it every Sunday: he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.
historical:
The heading, “A Psalm of David”, stands in the Hebrew as part of verse 1, so the verse numbers are the same in Hebrew and English. Most scholars classify Psalm 110 as a royal psalm from Jerusalem's court, probably delivered at a king's enthronement, when a prophet or priest spoke God's word to the new ruler. Its Hebrew is archaic and in places very difficult (verses 3, 6, and 7 especially), which many take as a sign of an early date during the monarchy. H. H. Rowley (in an essay on Melchizedek and Zadok published in 1950) proposed that it was composed soon after David took Jerusalem, and that it confirmed both David's rule and the priesthood of Zadok, whom Rowley took to be the city's old Jebusite priest.

A few scholars have dated it much later, to the Hasmonean rulers of the second and first centuries BC, who joined political leadership with the high priesthood. The Jewish people decreed in 140 BC that Simon, brother of Judas Maccabeus, should be their leader and high priest forever, until a trustworthy prophet should arise (1 Maccabees 14:41), language that resembles ‘a priest forever’. Robert Pfeiffer suggested that the psalm was written for Simon, and Marco Treves (Vetus Testamentum, 1965) claimed to find his name hidden as an acrostic in verses 1 to 4. Most scholars reject the Hasmonean date, because the acrostic requires selective reading and because the psalm's language and its use in the Psalter point much earlier. What the period does show is that the idea of a priest-king was alive and contested. The Testament of Moses (6:1), from the early first century AD, complains of kings who called themselves priests of the Most High God, and a decree of Augustus quoted by Josephus names ‘Hyrcanus, high priest of the Most High God’ (Antiquities 16.163), using Melchizedek's own title from Genesis 14.

Melchizedek links the psalm to Jerusalem's past. In Genesis 14:18-20 he is king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brings bread and wine to Abraham and blesses him, and Abraham gives him a tenth. Psalm 76:2 uses Salem as a name for Jerusalem, and the Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran (1QapGen 22:13) and Josephus (Antiquities 1.180; Jewish War 6.438) identify Salem with Jerusalem. When David captured Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:6-9), he inherited a city with a memory of priest-kings. David himself wore a linen ephod and offered sacrifices when he brought the ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:14, 17-18), and 2 Samuel 8:18 even calls his sons priests (kohanim), but the Davidic kings were not Levitical priests, and when King Uzziah tried to burn incense in the temple he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).

By the time of Jesus, Melchizedek had become a figure of speculation. Philo of Alexandria (Allegorical Interpretation 3.79-82) made him a picture of the divine Logos as priest. A fragmentary scroll from Qumran copied in the first century BC, 11QMelchizedek (11Q13), pictures him as a heavenly figure who proclaims a final jubilee of release, atones for the righteous, and carries out God's judgment on Belial and his spirits, applying to him texts such as Psalm 82:1; its surviving fragments do not quote Psalm 110. The book of 2 Enoch (chapters 71 and 72), whose date is debated, tells of Melchizedek's miraculous birth to an aged mother and his being taken to paradise before the flood. Hebrews 7 entered a conversation already under way, though it builds its case from the text of Genesis and the psalm rather than from these legends.
cultural:
To sit at a king's right hand was to hold the place of highest honor and delegated power; Solomon seats his mother Bathsheba at his right hand (1 Kings 2:19). In ancient Near Eastern art kings are shown enthroned beside or under the protection of their god, and defeated enemies lie beneath the king's feet. Othmar Keel's The Symbolism of the Biblical World (German 1972, English 1978) gathers many such images beside the Psalms. Among the footstools buried with the Egyptian king Tutankhamun (fourteenth century BC) are ones decorated with bound foreign captives, so that the king rested his feet on his enemies whenever he sat. Joshua has his captains put their feet on the necks of defeated kings (Joshua 10:24). Yet in Israel's own writing the word for footstool, hadom, is otherwise used of God's footstool: the ark (1 Chronicles 28:2), the temple (Psalm 99:5; 132:7; Lamentations 2:1), and the earth itself (Isaiah 66:1). The king's footstool in Psalm 110 is made by God.

The scepter (matteh) was the staff of office, the word used for Moses' staff (Exodus 4:20) and Aaron's rod that budded (Numbers 17:8). It goes out ‘from Zion’, the hill of the palace and the temple, so the king's rule flows from the place of God's presence. Verse 3 draws on the language of worship and war. The people are nedavot, literally ‘freewill offerings’: volunteers who give themselves, as the tribes who ‘offered themselves willingly’ for battle in Deborah's day (Judges 5:2, 9). ‘Holy splendor’ is the phrase used for the attire of worship (Psalm 29:2; 96:9). Dew in a land with no summer rain was the moisture that kept crops alive through the dry months, falling silently and everywhere at daybreak (2 Samuel 17:12; Hosea 14:5), a picture of freshness, abundance, and renewal.

The priest-king was a familiar figure in the ancient world. Assyrian kings called their reigns their priesthood and bore the title šangû, priest, of the god Ashur; Egyptian pharaohs were represented in temple reliefs as the chief priest of every god. Israel's law separated the offices: the king came from Judah, the priests from Levi and the house of Aaron. Psalm 110 does not merge them by borrowing from Israel's neighbors; it grounds the king's priesthood in a divine oath and in the older order of Melchizedek, who was priest before Levi was born.

An oath from God was the strongest form of commitment the Bible knows. God swears by himself to Abraham (Genesis 22:16), and swears to David that his line will endure (Psalm 89:35; 132:11). The addition ‘and will not change His mind’ closes off revision, as when Samuel says that the Glory of Israel does not change his mind, for he is not a man (1 Samuel 15:29). The last verse probably pictures a warrior who pauses in pursuit to drink from a streambed on the road, as Gideon's men drank at the spring of Harod (Judges 7:5-6), and lifts his head refreshed; some scholars instead connect it with a coronation rite at a spring, since Solomon was anointed at the Gihon spring below Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:38-40). To lift up the head is a Hebrew idiom for being vindicated and restored (Psalm 3:3; 27:6).
literary:
The psalm is built around two divine oracles, each followed by an expansion. The first oracle (verse 1) is an invitation to sit at God's right hand; verses 2 and 3 expand it with the scepter going out from Zion and the people volunteering on the day of battle. The second oracle (verse 4) is an oath that the king is a priest forever; verses 5 to 7 expand it with the day of wrath and the king's triumph. Each oracle is introduced with the LORD as speaker, and each ends with a picture of the king's victory. The whole poem runs only seven verses and moves from the throne room to the battlefield to a brook by the road.

The opening words, neum YHWH, ‘the utterance of the LORD’, are the formula of prophecy, used hundreds of times in the prophets (usually rendered ‘declares the LORD’) and nowhere else in the Psalms. The psalm presents itself as a prophetic word, not a courtier's compliment. The addressee is adoni, ‘my lord’, the form used for human superiors such as kings (1 Samuel 22:12), while verse 5 uses Adonai, the form reserved for God. The consonants of the two words are the same; the vowels added by the Masoretes (the medieval scribes who fixed the pronunciation of the Hebrew text) distinguish them, and their pointing agrees with how the words are used elsewhere. The Septuagint, which had no means to mark the difference, reads kyrios, ‘Lord’, for both.

The poem plays on position and on the word ‘head’. In verse 1 the king sits at God's right hand; in verse 5 the Lord is at the king's right hand, fighting for him, so that the two images frame the psalm's victories. The ‘day’ of the king's strength (verse 3) becomes the ‘day’ of the Lord's wrath (verse 5). In verse 6 God crushes the rosh, the head or chief, over the wide earth, and in verse 7 the king lifts up his rosh. The subject shifts without warning between the LORD and the king in verses 5 to 7, a feature interpreters resolve in different ways, and the same ambiguity has led Christian readers to hear the Father and the Son acting together. The most compressed line, verse 3, piles image on image (a willing people, holy splendor, the womb of the dawn, the dew of youth) in a way that has never been translated to everyone's satisfaction, and its obscurity is part of the psalm's air of ancient solemnity.

outline.t: First oracle: sit at my right hand
The scepter from Zion and a willing people
Second oracle: a priest forever like Melchizedek
The day of wrath and the king's triumph

doctrines.note: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (verse 1) is the Old Testament text behind the New Testament's confession that the risen Jesus has ascended and reigns at God's right hand (Acts 2:34-36; Ephesians 1:20; Hebrews 1:3, 13). The ‘until’ describes the present age: Christ already reigns, and his enemies are not yet all under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 10:12-13).

Verse 4 joins in one person the offices Israel's law kept apart: the king of verses 1 to 3 is declared “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews 5 to 7 builds on this to present Christ as the priest-king whose priesthood rests on God's oath and an indestructible life, and the Reformed doctrine of Christ's threefold office draws heavily on this psalm.

The psalm describes a king from David's line whom David himself calls ‘my lord’, who shares God's throne and rules from Zion. Jesus used verse 1 to show that the Messiah is more than David's son (Mark 12:35-37), and later Jewish tradition also applied the verse to the Messiah (Midrash on Psalms 18:29).

God's rule through his king is established but not yet complete. The king rules “in the midst of Your enemies” (verse 2), not after they have vanished, and his people come willingly (verse 3). The kingdom advances in a contested world, and its completion is left in God's hands (‘until I make’).

Verses 5 and 6 announce a day of wrath on which the Lord crushes kings and judges the nations. The psalm sets the king's priesthood beside his judgment: the one who intercedes forever is the one before whom the powers of the earth will give account.

words.note: Neum, utterance or declaration, a noun used about 376 times, almost always in the prophetic formula neum YHWH, ‘declares the LORD’ (Jeremiah alone has it more than 170 times). It also introduces the oracles of Balaam (Numbers 24:3-4, 15-16) and David's last words (2 Samuel 23:1). In the Psalms it appears only here with the divine name (Psalm 36:1 uses it of transgression speaking in the wicked heart). Its use in verse 1 marks the psalm as a prophetic oracle spoken on God's behalf.

Adon, lord, master, used more than three hundred times of human superiors: a master of slaves, a husband (Genesis 18:12), a king (1 Samuel 22:12; 1 Kings 1:17). The standard lexicons distinguish it from Adonai, the form used only of God. In verse 1 the LORD speaks ladoni, ‘to my lord’. Jesus' question in Mark 12:37 turns on this word: if David calls the Messiah ‘Lord’, how can the Messiah be merely his son? The title points to someone whose rank David acknowledges above his own.

Yamin, right hand, right side, used well over a hundred times. The right hand is the hand of strength and skill (“Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power”, Exodus 15:6), and the place at a ruler's right is the place of honor and delegated authority (1 Kings 2:19). The word frames this psalm: the king sits at God's right hand in verse 1, and the Lord is at the king's right hand in verse 5. The New Testament's many references to Christ at ‘the right hand of God’ all stand on this verse.

Hadom, footstool, only six times in the Hebrew Bible. Apart from this verse, it always names God's footstool: the ark of the covenant (1 Chronicles 28:2), the temple or Zion (Psalm 99:5; 132:7; Lamentations 2:1), and the whole earth (Isaiah 66:1). The phrase ‘footstool for Your feet’ in verse 1 therefore places the king's enemies beneath a footstool that God himself provides, and the image of total victory is borrowed from the royal art of the ancient Near East.

Nedavah, freewill offering, voluntariness, about twenty-six times. It names the offerings a worshiper brings not because the law requires them but out of a willing heart (Leviticus 7:16; Exodus 35:29), and the related verb describes people who volunteered for war or gave for the temple (Judges 5:2; 1 Chronicles 29:5-9). In verse 3 the king's people are ‘freewill offerings’ on his day of battle: they give themselves willingly, a picture Christian readers have applied to the church's response to Christ's reign.

Kohen, priest, about 750 times, the standard word for the sanctuary priest who offered sacrifices, taught the law, and blessed the people. In Israel the priests came from the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron (Exodus 28:1; Numbers 3:10), while the kings came from Judah. Declaring the king ‘a priest forever’ in verse 4 is therefore startling, and the psalm grounds it not in descent but in God's oath and in the older order of Melchizedek, whom Genesis 14:18 calls “priest of God Most High.”

Malkitsedeq, Melchizedek, a name that means ‘my king is righteousness’ or ‘king of righteousness’, the sense Hebrews 7:2 draws from it. He appears in the Old Testament only in Genesis 14:18-20 and here. The phrase ‘in the order of’ (al-divrati) uses a rare form that elsewhere means ‘on account of’ or ‘concerning’ (Ecclesiastes 3:18); most translators take it as ‘after the manner of’, a priesthood of Melchizedek's kind. The Septuagint's ‘according to the order (taxis) of Melchizedek’ is the wording Hebrews quotes.

Shava, to swear an oath, about 186 times, used of people swearing by God and, strikingly, of God swearing by himself (Genesis 22:16; Isaiah 45:23). In verse 4 the LORD ‘has sworn and will not change His mind’, joining the oath with nacham, ‘to relent’, negated. Hebrews 7:20-22 argues that because Christ's priesthood rests on such an oath, which the Levitical priests never received, it is the guarantee of a better covenant.

christ:
Psalm 110 is the Old Testament text the New Testament uses most to say who Jesus is and where he is now. Its first verse is quoted or clearly echoed in every major part of the New Testament, and its fourth verse carries the central argument of Hebrews.

Jesus himself raised the psalm. Teaching in the temple, he asked how the scribes could say the Messiah is David's son, when “Speaking by the Holy Spirit, David himself declared: ‘The Lord said to my Lord’” (Mark 12:36), and he pressed the point: “David himself calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David's son?” (Mark 12:37). The question implies that the Messiah is more than a human successor to David. At his trial Jesus joined the psalm to Daniel 7:13, telling the high priest that he would see “the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62), a claim the council heard as blasphemy.

After Easter the apostles read the resurrection and ascension as the fulfillment of verse 1. At Pentecost Peter argued that David did not ascend into heaven, so the one invited to sit at God's right hand must be someone else: “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). Stephen, dying, sees the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56). Paul says that Christ is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:34) and that “He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25), combining the psalm with Psalm 8:6. Ephesians 1:20, Colossians 3:1, 1 Peter 3:22, and Hebrews 1:3 and 1:13 all use the same language. David Hay's study Glory at the Right Hand (1973) catalogues these quotations and allusions and their use in early Christian writing.

Hebrews gives verse 4 its fullest reading. It quotes the line in 5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:17, and 7:21, and it draws three things from it. ‘Forever’ shows that this priesthood, unlike Aaron's, is not ended by death; Jesus has become a priest “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16), and “He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25). ‘Sworn’ shows that it rests on God's oath, which the Levitical priests never received (7:20-22). ‘Melchizedek’ shows that God appointed a priesthood outside Levi, which implies that the law under which Levi served has been changed (7:11-12). Hebrews also joins the two halves of the psalm: “when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God,” where he waits for his enemies to be made a footstool (Hebrews 10:12-13). The seated priest is the sign that the sacrifice is finished.

Here the link is not only thematic. The New Testament writers read the psalm as speaking directly of the Messiah, and Jesus himself taught them to. The church's confession that Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father, in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, and its teaching that he is both king and priest, rest on this psalm.
interpretation:
Jewish interpretation took several paths. Justin Martyr, writing his Dialogue with Trypho around 155 to 160, reports Jewish teachers who applied the psalm to King Hezekiah (chapters 33 and 83). The Babylonian Talmud (Nedarim 32b) reads it of Abraham after his victory over the kings in Genesis 14: Melchizedek, identified with Noah's son Shem, blessed Abraham before blessing God, and so the priesthood was taken from him and given to Abraham's descendants, a reading that turns ‘in the order of’ into ‘because of the words of’ Melchizedek. Rashi followed the Abraham reading while admitting that the mention of Zion, the city of David, is a difficulty for it. Abraham ibn Ezra read the psalm as spoken about David by one of the temple singers. The Midrash on Psalms (at Psalm 18:29) preserves a saying in the name of Rabbi Yudan that in the age to come God will seat the King Messiah at his right hand, quoting verse 1, and Abraham at his left.

Christian writers took the psalm from the beginning as a word about Christ. 1 Clement (about AD 96) quotes verse 1 of the Son (36:5). The church fathers used verse 3 in its Septuagint form, ‘from the womb before the morning star I begot you’, for the Son's eternal generation, and Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms treat the whole psalm as a summary of the faith. Theodore of Mopsuestia, who read most psalms historically, counted this one among the four that speak directly of Christ. Epiphanius of Salamis (Panarion 55) describes a group called Melchizedekians who ranked Melchizedek above Christ, an early sign of the speculation the name invites. Luther preached eight sermons on Psalm 110 in 1535, treating it as a chief psalm of Christ's kingdom and priesthood, and Calvin's commentary (1557) read it as David's prophecy of Christ, arguing that it cannot be applied to David or any other earthly king.

Modern critical scholarship, following Gunkel and Mowinckel, has read the psalm as a coronation oracle for a Davidic king, spoken by a court prophet, with scholars differing over its date (H. H. Rowley's Davidic setting in 1950 on one side, the rare Hasmonean proposals of Pfeiffer and Treves on the other). New Testament scholars have traced how early and how central the Christian reading was: David Hay's Glory at the Right Hand: Psalm 110 in Early Christianity (1973) and Martin Hengel's essay on Psalm 110:1, titled with the verse's opening words, in his Studies in Early Christology (1995) argue that the psalm shaped Christian confession of Jesus' exaltation within the first years after Easter.

The psalm has a rich life in worship. The confession in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds that Christ ‘sits at the right hand of the Father’ and the Te Deum's ‘You are seated at God's right hand’ both come from verse 1. In the Western Office it is the first psalm of Sunday Vespers, known by its Latin opening, Dixit Dominus, and so it has been set by many composers: Monteverdi in his Vespers of 1610, Handel in his Dixit Dominus written in Rome in 1707, Vivaldi, and Mozart in both his Vesperae de Dominica (1779) and Vesperae solennes de confessore (1780).
text:
Psalm 110 has the same verse numbers in Hebrew and English, because the heading is part of verse 1 in both. The Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate number it Psalm 109, because they join Psalms 9 and 10, which is why the Latin settings are often labeled ‘Psalm 109’.

In verse 1 the Hebrew distinguishes YHWH, ‘the LORD’, from adoni, ‘my lord’; the Septuagint has kyrios for both, and the New Testament quotations follow the Greek. Mark 12:36 and Matthew 22:44 read ‘under Your feet’, probably under the influence of Psalm 8:6, where Luke 20:43 and Acts 2:35 keep the Septuagint's ‘a footstool for Your feet’.

Verse 3 is where English Bibles differ most, because the Hebrew is compressed and the ancient versions read it differently. The Masoretic Text reads roughly ‘your people are freewill offerings on the day of your strength, in holy splendor; from the womb of the dawn, yours is the dew of your youth’. Several Hebrew manuscripts, and Jerome's translation from the Hebrew, read ‘on the holy mountains’ (beharerei) instead of ‘in holy splendor’ (behadrei); in Hebrew script the letters d and r are nearly identical. The Septuagint reads the consonants in yet another way: ‘with you is rule on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb before the morning star I begot you’, taking the last word as the verb of Psalm 2:7. The Latin Vulgate follows it, and much patristic and medieval theology of the Son's eternal generation rests on this Greek and Latin form. English versions follow the Hebrew but construe it variously: the BSB's ‘Your people shall be willing’, the ESV's ‘Your people will offer themselves freely’, and the NRSV's ‘Your people will offer themselves willingly’.

In verse 4 al-divrati is a rare phrase; the Septuagint's ‘according to the order of’ (kata ten taxin) is the reading behind Hebrews and most English versions, while the Talmud's reading ‘on account of the words of’ lies behind the Abraham interpretation. In verse 6 the line can be read ‘He will crush the leaders far and wide’ (BSB) or ‘he will shatter the head over the wide earth’, since rosh is singular. In verses 5 to 7 the subject is not marked, and translations differ over whether ‘the Lord’ of verse 5 is God fighting for the king or the king himself addressed to God.

teach.big: God has enthroned his King at his right hand and sworn that he is a priest forever, so the reign of the crucified and risen Jesus is certain even while it advances in the midst of enemies.

outline.t: God himself enthrones the Messiah at his right hand, a Lord whom David acknowledges above himself, and the ‘until’ tells us we live between the enthronement and the final victory.
Christ's rule goes out from Zion and is exercised in the midst of opposition, and his people come to him as freewill offerings, not conscripts.
By an oath God will never revoke, the King is also a priest forever, of an order older than Levi, so that his intercession for his people never ends.
The day of the King's victory is also a day of judgment on every power that resists God, and the King, refreshed on the road, lifts his head in triumph.

teach.pitfalls:
Three misuses recur. The first reads verses 5 and 6 as a license for holy war or for any nation's armies. The psalm's battle belongs to the Lord and his anointed, and the New Testament reads it as Christ's reign over every power, including the church's own enemies within and the ‘last enemy’, death (1 Corinthians 15:25-26). Preaching that casts a political or military cause as the king's willing army misuses verse 3 in the same way. The second misuse fills Melchizedek with speculation. Some preachers present him as an appearance of the preexistent Christ; Hebrews says instead that he was “like the Son of God” (Hebrews 7:3), and its argument rests on what Genesis does and does not say, not on hidden identities. The third overreads the Hebrew vowels of verse 1, as if the Masoretes had deliberately disguised a divine title; adoni is the ordinary form for a human lord, and Jesus' argument does not need a divine title in the verse, only that David calls his descendant ‘lord’.

Teachers should also keep the ‘until’ of verse 1. It is easy to preach Christ's reign as either wholly future or already complete; the psalm holds both, a king already seated and enemies not yet under his feet. And the priesthood of verse 4 should not be preached only as doctrine. Hebrews draws from it the practical consequence that believers can approach God with confidence, because the priest who sits at God's right hand lives to intercede for them.
teach.pastoral: Verse 4, read with Hebrews 7:25, speaks directly to believers troubled by guilt and scrupulosity, who fear that they have exhausted God's mercy or that their prayers are not enough. The psalm answers that their standing rests on a priest who holds office by God's oath and “always lives to intercede for them.” It also speaks to people living among hostile powers, who need to hear that Christ reigns “in the midst of Your enemies,” not only after the enemies are gone.

hard.q: Is “my Lord” in verse 1 the Messiah, as Jesus argues in Mark 12, or an ordinary king addressed by a court poet?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. Jewish interpreters have long read ‘my lord’ as a human figure: Justin Martyr reports second-century Jewish teachers who applied it to Hezekiah, the Talmud (Nedarim 32b) and Rashi to Abraham, and Abraham ibn Ezra to David spoken of by a temple singer. The Hebrew vowels support a human addressee, since adoni is the form used of human superiors, and the psalm says nothing explicit about a coming king. Modern critical scholars, from Hermann Gunkel onward, generally read the psalm as a coronation oracle in which a court prophet addresses the reigning king as ‘my lord’, and they read the heading ‘of David’ as meaning ‘for’ or ‘belonging to’ the Davidic king rather than ‘written by David’. On that reading Jesus' argument in Mark 12:35-37, which assumes that David himself is speaking about someone greater than himself, rests on an authorship the psalm does not require, and some critics conclude that the argument fails or that the scene reflects later Christian debate rather than Jesus' own teaching.

Several responses are made. The heading ‘A Psalm of David’ was understood as authorship in Jesus' time by both sides of the debate in Mark 12, and neither the scribes nor any later Jewish opponent in the Gospels challenges that premise. Luther (in his sermons of 1535) and Calvin (commentary, 1557) defended Davidic authorship and a direct prophetic reference, pointing to the prophetic formula neum YHWH, the eternal priesthood, and the enthronement at God's right hand as more than any son of David ever received. Many interpreters who accept a court setting argue that the psalm, like other royal psalms, said more than any historical king fulfilled, so that once the monarchy ended its promise pointed forward; this is how Jewish tradition itself could apply verse 1 to the Messiah (Midrash on Psalms 18:29), and how Qumran and other Second Temple writers came to speculate about a heavenly priest-king. David Hay (1973) and Martin Hengel (1995) show that the messianic reading was not a late Christian invention but among the earliest things the first Jewish believers in Jesus said about him.

Readers who hold a high view of Scripture differ over whether David wrote the psalm or a prophet addressed David's heir. They agree that the psalm speaks of a king whom God enthrones beside himself and swears to be a priest forever, and the church confesses as a first-order truth that Jesus is that King and Priest. The question of the psalm's first setting remains open.

hard.q: Is the argument of Hebrews about Melchizedek a fair reading of Genesis 14 and this psalm?
hard.a:
The objection is that Hebrews builds a great deal on very little. Genesis 14 gives Melchizedek three verses and says nothing about his parents or his death, yet Hebrews 7:3 describes him as “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God.” Critics see here an argument from silence of the kind common in Jewish exegesis of the period, the principle that what Scripture does not mention does not exist, used to reach a conclusion the original texts never intended. Jewish tradition read the same texts in the opposite direction: the Talmud (Nedarim 32b) holds that Melchizedek's priesthood was taken from him and given to Abraham's line, so that Levi's priesthood is the heir of Melchizedek's, not its inferior. Philo read Melchizedek as an allegory of the Logos, and 11QMelchizedek made him a heavenly redeemer, which shows how widely the figure could be bent to an interpreter's purpose.

Responses begin with what Hebrews actually claims. Commentators such as F. F. Bruce (New International Commentary, 1964) and Harold Attridge (Hermeneia, 1989) note that Hebrews knowingly uses the argument from the silence of Scripture, and that it does not say Melchizedek was literally eternal; it says he is “like the Son of God” in the way Scripture presents him, a type rather than a double. More importantly, the load-bearing words of Hebrews 7 come from the psalm, not from Genesis: ‘forever’, ‘sworn’, and ‘in the order of Melchizedek’. The psalm itself, centuries before Hebrews, had already drawn a priesthood out of Genesis 14 that was separate from Levi and permanent by oath, so Hebrews is extending a reading that begins inside the Old Testament. The Qumran and Philonic parallels show that Hebrews wrote within a lively Jewish conversation, and its restraint is notable beside them: it makes no claims about Melchizedek's heavenly nature and focuses on Jesus, whose priesthood depends on “the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16).

Christians agree that Hebrews is inspired Scripture and differ on how to describe its method: some stress its continuity with the plain sense of the Old Testament, others its use of the interpretive techniques of its day. Both readings hold that the psalm's oath is the ground of Christ's priesthood.

observe: The LORD speaks twice in this psalm, in verse 1 and verse 4. What does he say each time, and what form does the second word take?
Where is the king in verse 1, and where is the Lord in verse 5? What changes between the two pictures?
What images describe the king's people in verse 3, and what do they suggest about how they come to him?
interpret: Jesus asked how David's son could also be David's Lord (Mark 12:35-37). What answer does the rest of the New Testament give to his question?
Why does the psalm ground the king's priesthood in an oath and in Melchizedek rather than in the family of Aaron, and why does that matter to Hebrews?
What does the word ‘until’ in verse 1 imply about the time between Christ's enthronement and his final victory?
apply: Christ reigns “in the midst of Your enemies.” Where do you need to trust his rule while opposition is still present?
Hebrews says the priest of Psalm 110 always lives to intercede for his people. How should that shape the way you pray when you feel your prayers are weak?
The king's people offer themselves willingly on his day. What would it look like for you to serve Christ as a freewill offering rather than out of obligation?
